domain: Religious Studies / Comparative Religion / Japanese History
topic_summary: Analysis of shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) in pre-Meiji Japan, examining whether centuries of simultaneous practice represent a single fused commitment or domain-partitioned coexistence. The kernel contest tests whether 'one-syncretic-kernel' and 'domain-partition' readings cohere or expose structural incoherence in what appeared as unified practice.

key_entities: Honji-suijaku theory (interpretive framework: kami as local manifestations of universal buddhas)
Meiji government (1868+ state authority enforcing shinbutsu-bunri separation)
Jingu-ji temples (institutional sites housing both kami shrines and Buddhist halls)
key_tensions: Ontological unity vs functional partition (whether kami and buddhas are same beings or domain-specialized entities)
Elite interpretation vs popular practice (honji-suijaku theory vs lay ritual behavior)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that kami and buddhas can be simultaneously venerated without contradiction
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy distributed across Buddhist clergy (honji-suijaku doctrine), shrine priests (kami ritual specialists), and popular practice (ritual pragmatism)

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are ontologically identical beings viewed through different cultural lenses; honji-suijaku theory captures metaphysical truth
readings.expected_structural_delta: Single constraint with high ε (ontological unity enforced); beneficiary: Buddhist institutional hierarchy claiming interpretive monopoly; victim: indigenous kami autonomy

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are functionally distinct entities governing separate domains (this-worldly prosperity vs afterlife salvation); simultaneous veneration is domain-appropriate specialization
readings.authority_grounding: Popular practice norms and shrine-temple institutional division of labor
readings.expected_structural_delta: Two parallel constraints (life-domain kami constraint + death-domain buddha constraint) with independent ε values; no beneficiary extraction, coordination rope structure

readings.commitment: Simultaneous veneration was never coherent; practitioners held contradictory beliefs simultaneously without resolution, sustained by lack of enforcement pressure until Meiji separation
readings.authority_grounding: Meiji-era rationalist critique and modern religious studies skepticism of syncretism coherence
readings.expected_structural_delta: No stable constraint; high ε from suppressed contradiction; Meiji shinbutsu-bunri as revelation of latent incoherence rather than imposed rupture

axes.human_readable: Ontological Fusion Reading (Honji-Suijaku as Metaphysical Truth)
axes.structural_delta: Kami and buddhas are identical beings; honji-suijaku theory enforces ontological unity
axes.primary_observable: Prevalence of honji-suijaku doctrine in temple records; institutional merger of shrine-temple complexes
axes.selection_reason: Highest institutional authority grounding; tangled_rope structure with clear beneficiary extraction

axes.human_readable: Domain Partition Reading (Functional Specialization Without Ontological Claim)
axes.structural_delta: Kami govern this-worldly prosperity, buddhas govern afterlife; simultaneous veneration is domain-appropriate coordination
axes.primary_observable: Ritual context analysis (birth/harvest rituals at shrines vs funeral/memorial rituals at temples); lay practitioner testimony
axes.selection_reason: Structurally distinct from fusion reading (coordination vs extraction); grounded in popular practice rather than elite doctrine

axes.human_readable: Pragmatic Incoherence Reading (Sustained Contradiction Until Meiji Enforcement)
axes.structural_delta: Simultaneous veneration was never coherent; practitioners held contradictory beliefs without resolution
axes.primary_observable: Meiji shinbutsu-bunri enforcement success rate; speed of shrine-temple separation; lack of popular resistance
axes.selection_reason: Highest centrality; tests whether kernel itself is coherent or a suppressed contradiction; Meiji separation as natural experiment

axes.human_readable: Institutional Merger as Physical Constraint (Jingu-ji Architecture)
axes.structural_delta: Physical co-location of shrines and temples in jingu-ji complexes created path-dependent fusion
axes.primary_observable: Architectural records of jingu-ji sites; cost of separation during Meiji period
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: upstream physical constraint but lower structural distinctiveness than selected readings; captured implicitly in fusion/partition readings

axes.human_readable: Meiji Shinbutsu-Bunri as Coherence Test (State-Imposed Separation)
axes.structural_delta: Meiji government separation policy as natural experiment revealing whether syncretism was stable or suppressed incoherence
axes.primary_observable: Resistance patterns to separation edicts; speed of compliance; post-separation practice continuity
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: downstream test of kernel coherence but redundant with pragmatic_incoherence_reading which already incorporates Meiji separation as evidence

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Physical co-location in jingu-ji complexes created path-dependent fusion
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Upstream physical constraint captured implicitly in selected readings; lower structural distinctiveness

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Meiji separation policy as natural experiment testing syncretism stability
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Downstream test redundant with pragmatic_incoherence_reading which already incorporates Meiji evidence

omegas.description: Do the three readings genuinely emit different constraints, or do fusion and partition readings collapse into the same observable (ritual behavior) with different post-hoc rationalizations? If collapse occurs, the kernel is incoherent and should be reclassified as a single axis with contested interpretation rather than contested constraint.
omegas.source: §1.3-K coherence test; D2 half-break deliberate probe

omegas.description: If Meiji separation had not occurred, would shinbutsu-shugo have persisted indefinitely or collapsed under internal contradiction? Pragmatic_incoherence_reading depends on Meiji as revealing latent instability, but absence of separation might have sustained indefinite coexistence.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory): no internal enforcement mechanism prior to Meiji

omegas.description: Elite honji-suijaku doctrine vs popular domain-partition practice may represent two non-communicating systems rather than two readings of one kernel. If so, the kernel is not contested but fragmented across social strata.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan): Buddhist clergy benefit from fusion reading; popular practitioners may have operated under partition reading without awareness of doctrinal conflict

omegas.description: Model's training on English-language religious studies scholarship may overweight Meiji-era rationalist critiques and underweight Japanese-language primary sources on pre-Meiji practice. Pragmatic_incoherence_reading may reflect scholarly bias rather than historical reality.
omegas.source: F34 (Epistemic Trespass) concern: limited access to pre-Meiji Japanese primary sources
